name: PT Nitrasanata Dharma

frontmatter.title: JEC Eye Hospitals: a good franchise priced for a recovery that has not started
frontmatter.summary: We initiate JECX at SELL. JEC is the largest dedicated eye-hospital chain in Indonesia, but the 2026 accounts show profit down on a flat top line while the shares trade at a multiple that assumes the margin recovery is already banked. Our DCF, built on the reported cost base and the company's own expansion plan, gives a target well below the market price.
thesis: The franchise is real: five eye hospitals and eleven clinics, a brand built over four decades, and a one-stop clinical model that general hospitals cannot easily replicate [S5][S12].

The earnings are not: operating profit fell in the first half of 2026 on revenue that grew only modestly, because the cost base added for the 2023-25 openings is still running ahead of their revenue [S9].
The price assumes the recovery: the reverse DCF needs revenue growth far above both our forecast and the run-rate the company is actually delivering [S0].
The balance sheet is fixed by the IPO: new money repaid the bank debt, so interest cost collapses even if nothing else improves [S3][S5].
The controlling group is buying, not selling: SAME raised its stake and insiders bought at prices above today's, which caps the downside but does not create the earnings [S6][S7].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited accounts: the first full-year test of whether the opex ratio has peaked
First post-IPO dividend decision, against the pre-IPO distribution record
JEC Bali @ Sanur eye clinic in KEK Sanur: opening and ramp of the medical-tourism project
Monthly insider and controller shareholding disclosures continue to track conviction

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Nitrasanata Dharma Tbk, which trades as JEC Eye Hospitals & Clinics, with a **SELL** rating and a target price of **Rp647** against a last price of Rp935, a total return of -30.0%. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in July 2026 and has since fallen from its first-day peak of Rp1,950 to Rp935; the market capitalisation is IDR3,041.8bn on a free float of 20.8% [S5][S0].

The business is the best-known dedicated eye-care brand in the country: five eye hospitals and eleven eye clinics across Jabodetabek, Central Java, East Java, Bali and Sulawesi, built on a clinical model that keeps the patient inside one specialist network from diagnosis to surgery [S5]. Nothing in our work disputes the franchise. What we dispute is the price. At the last close the shares carry a price-earnings multiple of 45.0x on our FY2026E earnings and 16.7x enterprise value to EBITDA on the last audited balance sheet, for a company whose first-half operating profit was 49.9 IDR bn against 58.9 IDR bn a year earlier, on revenue that rose only to 459 IDR bn from 444 IDR bn [S9][S0].

Our variant view is that the margin trough is later and shallower than the market assumes. The cost base stepped up when the new hospitals opened ahead of their revenue and has not yet come down: general and administrative expense alone was 218 IDR bn in the first half of 2026 [S9]. We think that base does unwind as those facilities mature, which is why our FY2027E earnings rise sharply to Rp30 per share from Rp21; but the unwind is a two-to-three year process, not a switch the market can capitalise today. The reverse DCF makes the gap explicit: to justify the current price on our discount rate and terminal assumptions, FY2027E revenue growth would have to be 15.0%, against the 8.0% we forecast and the low single-digit growth the company actually delivered through September 2026 [S0].

Two things genuinely support the shares and we do not dismiss them. First, the IPO repaid the bank debt, so interest expense falls from the FY2026E level of roughly the current charge to a much smaller number thereafter; gross debt was down to IDR88.6bn in our forecast from IDR325.6bn at the end of FY2025 [S0][S3]. Second, the controlling group is a buyer: SAME, the Emtek-controlled hospital operator, lifted its stake to 30.1% and spent 107 IDR bn in a single week in July at prices between the IPO price and the first-day peak, while a commissioner and an unidentified shareholder bought at 905 IDR per share in November, parcels small enough to be noise [S7][S6]. A controlling shareholder accumulating above the market price is a floor under sentiment, not under earnings.

What moves the value, in order: the pace at which the opex ratio falls (each point of SG&A is worth materially more than a point of revenue growth at this margin), the revenue path of the hospital network including the Bali project, and the discount rate with the terminal growth rate behind it. The interest saving from the IPO is a real effect on earnings but not a free-cash-flow driver: the DCF is struck before interest, so the saving reaches the target only through the price-earnings cross-check, where it lifts earnings per share and the multiple-based value. Our bear and bull cases shock the operating drivers in opposite directions.

JEC began in 1984 as Klinik Mata Jakarta and has operated for four decades as a dedicated eye hospital, converting from a clinic into a hospital and then into a network [S12]. It listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange on 7 July 2026 at an offer price of 1,250 IDR per share, raising new money alongside a divestment by an existing shareholder; the offer was fifteen per cent of the post-IPO capital [S4][S5].

The operating footprint at the time of listing was 5.0 hospitals eye hospitals and 11.0 clinics eye clinics, spread from Jabodetabek through Central Java, East Java and Bali to Sulawesi [S5]. The company describes a one-stop model in which cataract, refractive, vitreoretinal, glaucoma, paediatric ophthalmology and low-vision care are delivered inside one network rather than referred out, supported by what it calls a hospitel concept that adds hotel-style comfort to inpatient care [S12]. It holds paripurna accreditation from the hospital accreditation committee, is a founding member of the ASEAN Association of Eye Hospitals and an active member of the World Association of Eye Hospitals, and its clinicians and technology are the basis of the brand it sells [S12]. The group employed 1,170.0 people at the last count [S0].

Revenue is effectively one business line. The company does not publish a segment split in the material we could reach, and the data pack carries a single revenue line, so we model one operating segment: private eye care, with a mix of self-pay, insurer and national health-insurance patients [S0][S5]. The clinics act as feeders into the hospitals for surgery, which is why the network economics depend on throughput per facility rather than on price alone.

The strategy since the IPO has three parts. The first is to fill the capacity already built: several hospitals opened in the years before listing and are still maturing. The second is geographic extension, with the JEC Bali @ Sanur eye clinic in the Sanur special economic zone explicitly aimed at the medical-tourism segment [S5]. The third is balance-sheet repair: the new money was earmarked to prepay bank principal and to fund subsidiaries and working capital [S3]. Management has not published numeric medium-term targets in the sources we could reach, and we do not invent them; our forecast is built from the reported run-rate and the disclosed project list.

Ownership is concentrated but not opaque at the top. SAME, the listed hospital operator controlled by the Emtek group, holds 30.1% after buying through the market in July and August 2026 [S7]. Magna Selaras Lestari is described as the controller, with a stake of 9.2% after its November purchases, and the ultimate beneficial owner is identified as Darwan Madja Purba [S3][S6]. A controller holding a minority of the shares while a strategic shareholder holds the largest block is a structure that depends on concert-party arrangements we cannot verify from public filings, and we treat it as a governance observation rather than a control fact.

Indonesian eye care is a demand story before it is a price story. The Ministry of Health is targeting a cataract surgical rate of 3,000 operations per million population a year, which is an explicit statement that the country is under-operating relative to the disease burden [S11]. The same ministry describes vision disorders as a leading source of disability and frames the backlog as an ageing-population problem, with a national roadmap to expand screening and surgical coverage [S11]. For a specialist chain, that is a volume tailwind that does not depend on consumer confidence.

Cataract surgery is the highest-volume procedure in ophthalmology and the one most sensitive to capacity rather than to fashion. Refractive surgery, retina and glaucoma care carry higher tickets but smaller volumes. In most emerging markets the binding constraint is the supply of ophthalmologists and operating theatres, not patient willingness to pay, which is why chains that train and retain specialists grow faster than the underlying market.

The regulatory frame matters more than the demographic one. A large part of Indonesian hospital revenue runs through the national health insurer, whose tariff schedule is set administratively; private chains protect margin by growing the insured and self-pay mix and by keeping equipment utilisation high. We have not found a source that quantifies JEC's payer mix, and we flag that as a gap rather than assume it. What we can say is that the company serves both national-insurance and private patients across its network, and that its hospital formats include one explicitly designed for national-insurance and self-pay volume [S12].

Competition comes from two directions. General private hospital groups run ophthalmology departments and capture the patient who is already inside their building; dedicated eye chains capture the patient who is shopping for a specialist. JEC is the largest dedicated chain we can identify, with the brand recognition that comes from four decades of operation and repeated external recognition [S12]. We could not source a market-share figure for eye care in Indonesia, and we do not present one. The moat we are willing to underwrite is narrower and more defensible: doctor networks and training, equipment intensity that a small clinic cannot match, and a brand that supports a price premium in self-pay. None of those is a network effect, and none of them protects against a well-capitalised general hospital group deciding to compete harder.

On the five forces: supplier power is moderate and rising with the rupiah, because much of the diagnostic and surgical equipment is imported; buyer power is high for national-insurance volume and moderate for self-pay; the threat of new entrants is real at clinic level and low at hospital level because of capital and specialist scarcity; substitutes are public hospitals and, for refractive work, overseas centres; and rivalry is increasing as private capacity is added across the sector [S5][S11]. That mix supports a mid-teens operating margin at maturity, not the low-twenties the company earned when it was smaller, which is exactly the shape of our forecast [S0].

External influences are mostly imported cost and the currency. The house macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD against the dollar in FY2027E, which raises the local-currency cost of equipment and consumables faster than the tariff schedule is likely to move [S0]. We do not model it, because we have no sourced split of imported consumables in cost of sales and no disclosed hedging policy; the gross margin is held at the reported level, so the exposure sits in the risk section rather than in the base case.

The reported history is short: the data pack carries three fiscal years, FY2023A to FY2025A, and four quarters, so we describe a three-year record rather than implying a longer one [S0]. Revenue rose from IDR825.1bn in FY2023A to IDR926.8bn in FY2025A, a slow compound, while EBITDA fell from IDR216.2bn to IDR196.2bn over the same period [S0]. The cause is visible in the cost lines rather than the gross margin: gross margin held at 61.2% of revenue, but operating expense rose from IDR337.6bn to IDR448.0bn, taking the operating margin from the low twenties to the low teens [S0]. Net profit attributable to the owners of the parent was IDR73.8bn in FY2025A [S15]. That line and the minority share behind it are restated from the audited income statement rather than taken from the data pack: the pack's net-profit line is group profit, including the non-controlling interest, and it records a zero minority share in every year. The audited statement splits the two, with the non-controlling interest taking IDR13.2bn in FY2023A (a gain, from the subsidiaries that were profit-making before the 2024-25 openings) and small losses of IDR-2.5bn and IDR-1.3bn in FY2024A and FY2025A respectively [S15]. We carry the LK series, so the P/E cross-check in the valuation section reads the parent base it claims to read.

The 2026 interim accounts continue the same pattern. First-half revenue was 459 IDR bn, up from 444 IDR bn, but operating profit fell to 49.9 IDR bn from 58.9 IDR bn and net profit attributable to shareholders fell to 18.9 IDR bn from 30.3 IDR bn [S9]. The company attributes the decline to higher marketing and general and administrative expense, and the numbers bear that out: G&A was 218 IDR bn and marketing expense rose alongside it [S9]. Pre-tax profit fell to 34.6 IDR bn, and total liabilities rose to 828 IDR bn against total assets of 1,530 IDR bn as the IPO balance sheet was assembled [S9]. The September quarter was flat on the prior year at the revenue line and better at the gross margin, which is the first evidence that the cost base is peaking [S0].

Our FY2026E revenue is IDR949.0bn, growth of 2.4%, which is the arithmetic of the nine-month run-rate plus a seasonally softer fourth quarter, not a recovery assumption [S0]. We then grow revenue 8.0% in FY2027E and 8.0% in FY2028E as the clinics and hospitals already in the network mature - the Cibubur, Tambora, Cinere, Bekasi, Semarang, Purwokerto and Surabaya sites among them - and the Bali project contributes, fading to 7.0% by FY2030E and 4.0% in the long run [S12]. We hold the ramp at the level the network's own capacity and the Bali build support rather than the delivered run-rate, and we state the gap plainly: the company does not publish opening dates, beds or revenue per facility for the newer sites, so this is the largest unsourced lever in the model [S5][S12][S16]. The sensitivity table in the valuation section prices that lever directly: it carries a revenue-growth axis in points either side of our path, so a reader who thinks the ramp is too optimistic can read the cost of the assumption off the grid instead of taking our word for it. Gross margin is held at 61.2% and allowed to drift up to 62.2%, below the peak year, because the network is larger and carries more fixed clinical cost. The operating expense ratio is the single most important line in the model: 48.8% in FY2026E, falling to 44.5% by FY2030E as the new hospitals absorb the staff and administrative cost added for them. That fade is a BLOCK-flagged drift and our justification, with sources, sits in the assumptions file; the September quarter already shows the ratio below the first-half level, which is why we are willing to underwrite it [S0][S9].

EBITDA on that build is IDR186.0bn in FY2026E and IDR317.0bn in FY2030E, with net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR67.6bn and IDR157.5bn respectively. Earnings per share rise from Rp21 to Rp48. The interest line does much of the early work: gross debt falls to IDR88.6bn from IDR325.6bn as the IPO money prepays bank principal, so the interest charge drops from the FY2025A level of IDR26.9bn to roughly a quarter of it [S0][S3].

Cash conversion has been a strength and remains one. Operating cash flow exceeded net profit in each of the three reported years, and free cash flow to the firm was IDR70.0bn in FY2025A after a heavy capex year [S0]. Working capital is structurally negative, at -14.0% of revenue, because patient receivables from insurers are funded by trade and other payables; we hold that ratio rather than assume it reverses [S0]. Capex was IDR103.5bn in FY2025A after a much heavier FY2024A, and we carry 13.0% of revenue in FY2026E and 14.0% in FY2027E for the Bali build before fading to 10.0% of revenue by FY2030E and lower again in the long run as maintenance of the existing hospitals takes over [S0][S5]. On that combination, free cash flow to the firm is IDR19.9bn in FY2026E and IDR44.2bn in FY2027E: the company is not yet a cash compounder, because capex and tax absorb most of the EBITDA improvement.

Capital allocation is the weakest part of the story to underwrite. Pre-IPO the entity distributed most of its earnings to its four shareholders; post-IPO the stated use of the new money is debt repayment, subsidiary funding and working capital, and the Bali project needs capital [S3][S5]. We assume a payout of 40.0%, roughly half the historical ratio, and flag that this is our assumption rather than a published policy. The company has not declared a dividend since listing.

Four earnings-quality flags, in the order they matter. First, the data pack records no minority share of profit in any of the three reported years even though the group carries a minority interest of IDR144.4bn on the balance sheet [S0]. The audited income statement shows the pack is wrong on this line: the non-controlling interest took IDR13.2bn in FY2023A and small losses of IDR-2.5bn and IDR-1.3bn in the two following years, and parent profit was correspondingly IDR114.1bn, IDR65.0bn and IDR73.8bn rather than the pack's group totals [S15]. We restate both lines from the LK for all three years, so the model history now carries the audited parent series and the minority share. The forecast minority is held at zero: the non-controlling share has been a small loss in the two most recent years, no disclosed basis supports a positive share, and the line is immaterial to parent earnings at this level of group profit. Second, we could not open the depreciation note in the financial statements, and the pack's quarterly depreciation is erratic - a small charge in one quarter and a large one in the next - so we carry the annual ratio of 7.2% of revenue, which is consistent with the fixed-asset base, and say plainly that the level may understate the true charge [S0]. Third, the pack carries no dividend-per-share series at all, so we restate it from the audited note: the cash dividend approved at the annual meeting of 16 April 2025 works out at Rp21 per share over the weighted-average share count, and because such a meeting approves the preceding year, it was paid out of FY2024 retained earnings rather than out of FY2025 profit [S15]. That restatement restores the balance-sheet roll-forward, and it reverses the earlier working assumption that the company paid nothing. Fourth, one model limitation has to be stated plainly because it touches a displayed multiple. The template's cash line is an operating roll-forward from the audited 31 December 2025 balance sheet and carries no equity-financing line, so the new money raised in the July 2026 IPO - IDR406.6bn of primary proceeds, separate from the divestment tranche sold by existing shareholders [S3] - cannot be entered in it. The forecast therefore shows net debt where the reported 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows the group in net cash, and the model's own EV/EBITDA display is struck on that understated cash position. No valuation output depends on it: the discounted cash flow and both cross-checks take cash, debt and minorities from the reported September balance sheet [S0], which is the position the bridge in the valuation section reconciles to the December 2025 accounts, and the report no longer quotes the roll-forward-based multiple. We disclose the gap rather than restate a balance sheet we cannot source at the forecast date.

On the screens we run before committing estimates: the accruals ratio is negative rather than positive, with cash earnings above accounting earnings in every reported year, which is the good direction [S0]. Receivables have not outgrown revenue. There is no special-monitoring-board notation and no going-concern or late-filing letter; the company listed in July 2026 and its free float of 20.8% is above the exchange minimum [S0]. Related-party balances and transactions are affirmatively nil in the audited record: the related-party note states that the group had no significant related-party balances and entered into no significant related-party transactions in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 [S15]. That is a clean disclosure rather than a gap, but it stops at the December 2025 balance-sheet date, before SAME became a shareholder in August 2026, and no post-IPO related-party note is in the material we hold. SAME is both the largest shareholder and a competing hospital operator, which is a structural conflict to monitor rather than a finding [S7].

Hospitals are valued on cash flow first and on EBITDA second, and this one is no exception: the assets are long-lived, the revenue is contracted patient volume rather than a commodity price, and the earnings are capital-intensive enough that a multiple applied to EBITDA alone would ignore the capex needed to keep five hospitals current. We weight the discounted cash flow at 60%, enterprise value to EBITDA at 30% and price-earnings at 10%, the house convention for a compounder with a short listed history. A price-earnings cross-check carries little weight here because the earnings base is at a trough and because the company has only three reported years.

The cost of capital sits inside the house band for rupiah assets, and the arithmetic is written out because the last draft left a term out. We start from the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, deduct the 1.6% sovereign default spread the house macro deck applies to rupiah cash flows, add an unlevered beta of 0.70 - the industry default for hospitals - multiplied by the sum of the 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium and the 2.5% country risk premium, and add a 1.0% premium for a newly listed name. That gives a cost of equity of 11.6% and a weighted average cost of capital of 11.5% [S0]. The default-spread deduction is the term that makes the answer lower than the raw component sum, and a reader who rejects it should read the discount-rate rows of the sensitivity table, which show the value at the higher rate those components imply without it. Pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4% and the debt weight is only 0.03 of capital after the IPO repayment, so the discount rate is effectively an equity rate.

The primary method gives Rp505 per share. The forecast period runs to FY2035E, with terminal growth of 4.0%, below Indonesia's nominal GDP on the house macro deck but above consumer inflation, and the terminal value is 56.9% of the total. We hold it there deliberately: a mature hospital network should not be assumed to outgrow the economy, and a higher rate would imply an exit multiple above the sector median we use in the cross-check. The sensitivity table shows the value at the adjacent growth and discount rates, so the reader can see what a point of terminal growth is worth before rejecting the choice. The DCF assumes the operating expense ratio falls as described and capex normalises to maintenance plus the Bali project. Free cash flow to the firm is struck before interest, so the IPO's interest saving does not enter the discounted cash flow at all; it reaches the target only through the earnings that the price-earnings cross-check capitalises, which is why the investment summary ranks it as an earnings effect rather than a cash-flow driver. Its implied exit multiple is below the multiple at which the shares trade today, so the model embeds de-rating rather than multiple expansion; that is the correct posture for a premium-multiple Indonesian healthcare name given the sector's history.

The cross-checks straddle the DCF, and the larger gap is above the primary method, not below it. EV/EBITDA gives Rp759 per share at 12.4x, 50.3% above the discounted cash flow - a divergence wider than the house threshold that requires it to be discussed explicitly, so here is the driver. That leg applies a single peer multiple, not a blend. The house method for hospitals calls for an average of the peer median and the stock's own five-year average, but this stock listed in July 2026 and has no five-year trading history, so the blend branch never runs and the leg takes the peer median alone: 12.4x, which is the MTMH.JK enterprise-value-to-EBITDA multiple. The engine applies it to FY2025A EBITDA of IDR196.2bn, adds the net cash on the reported 30 September 2026 balance sheet and deducts the minority block at book - the standard enterprise-value-to-equity bridge. Two things make this the highest of the three methods. First, FY2025A is the last full year before the cost step-up from the 2023-25 hospital openings reached the profit and loss account, which takes our FY2026E EBITDA to IDR186.0bn - so the multiple is applied to a larger earnings base than the one we forecast. Second, the multiple itself carries the whole of the gap: the discounted cash flow's enterprise value of IDR1,605.5bn is what the forecast cash flows support, and the peer multiple applied to the pre-step-up EBITDA produces a materially larger enterprise value on the same net cash and the same minority deduction, so this is a disagreement about the rating the peer set commands, not an arithmetic difference to be averaged away. We keep the weights as specified - the primary method at 60% - rather than bend them toward the cross-check that happens to be highest. Price-earnings gives Rp449 at 19.8x on FY2025A parent earnings of IDR73.8bn, -11.0% below the DCF: that earnings base is the trough and still carries the pre-IPO interest charge the IPO removed [S3], so on our FY2027E earnings the same multiple would be worth materially more, which is the honest size of the deleveraging effect and the reason this weight stays small. The blended value today is Rp576, above the DCF only because the EV/EBITDA leg lifts it; the base case rolls forward to Rp634 and the probability-weighted target is Rp647, below the price on every method.

The net debt in that bridge is not the model's forecast cash line, and the reconciliation matters because the IPO money sits between the two dates. At 31 December 2025 the audited accounts show net debt of IDR81.5bn [S15]. The July 2026 IPO then raised IDR406.6bn of new money for the company, separate from the divestment tranche sold by existing shareholders [S3], and the stated uses were prepayments of IDR40.0bn to BCA and IDR100.0bn to HSBC Indonesia plus IDR185.0bn of injection into subsidiaries [S3]. Nine months of trading, capex and working-capital movement carry the balance to the reported 30 September 2026 position, where cash exceeds debt and the group is in net cash [S0]; that reported position, not the forecast roll-forward, is what the DCF and both cross-checks use. The forecast cash line is an operating roll-forward only: it starts from the December 2025 accounts and the template has no equity-financing line, so it cannot carry the primary proceeds. That is why the roll-forward-based display multiple is not the one quoted in this report, and why the financial analysis section discloses the gap rather than leaving it to be inferred.

The bridge deducts the minority interest at book, and that needs explaining because the forecast books no minority share of profit even though the audited history does. The DCF values consolidated free cash flow, which includes the subsidiaries the minority part-owns, so a deduction is required for consistency; deducting book equity is the only sub-level number the accounts give us, and it does not understate the deduction, since a block whose share of profit has been a small loss is worth no more than its book. We flag it as a placeholder for a subsidiary-level valuation we could not source, not as a haircut on the operating case [S15].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of our disagreement. Holding the discount rate, margins and terminal assumptions at our base case, the current price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 15.0% [S0]. We forecast 8.0%. The company grew revenue by single digits in each of the last two reported years and by less than that in the first nine months of 2026, so the price requires an acceleration that neither the reported numbers nor any disclosed plan supports. If the reader believes the Bali project and the maturing hospitals can deliver that acceleration, the bull case is the place to look, not the base case.
The risks that matter, with our likelihood and impact assessment:

**Margin recovery fails (high likelihood, high impact).** The entire forecast rests on the operating expense ratio falling. If the new hospitals take longer to mature, or if wage inflation outruns revenue, the operating margin stays near the current level and the DCF falls toward the bear case. This is the risk the red team should attack first.

**Payer and tariff regulation (medium, high).** A large share of Indonesian hospital volume runs through administratively priced national insurance. A tariff freeze or a change in the class structure compresses revenue per patient without a matching cost reduction [S11]. We have not sourced JEC's payer mix, so we cannot size this precisely, which is itself a reason to demand a discount.

**Currency and imported equipment (medium, medium).** The house macro deck has the rupiah weaker in FY2027E than today, and diagnostic and surgical equipment is imported; a weaker currency raises the cost of the technology that underpins the brand [S0].

**Execution at JEC Bali @ Sanur (medium, medium).** The medical-tourism project is new territory for a domestic self-pay franchise: it needs international accreditation, foreign referral channels and a different price point [S5]. A delayed opening pushes revenue out without pushing cost out.

**Governance and related parties (low-to-medium, medium).** SAME is the largest shareholder and a competing hospital operator, and the controller holds a smaller stake than SAME [S7][S6]. Related-party transactions with either are the channel through which value could leak. The audited accounts state that the group had no significant related-party balances and entered into no significant related-party transactions in FY2023 to FY2025 per the related-party note [S15], so the historical record is clean; the exposure that is not covered is the post-IPO period, from the July 2026 listing and SAME's August 2026 purchases onward, for which we hold no related-party disclosure.

**Lock-up expiry (medium, medium).** The July 2026 IPO sold fifteen per cent of the capital and the register is concentrated: SAME, Darwan Madja Purba, Magna Selaras Lestari and the other pre-IPO holders own almost everything not sold [S3][S5][S6][S7]. Pre-IPO holders are locked for eight months after the registration statement becomes effective, as the prospectus states, so the first supply event falls around March 2027, inside our forecast horizon, against a float of 20.8% [S16]. We carry it as a signpost rather than a model input.

**Control and tender optionality (medium, medium).** SAME is a competing hospital operator and the largest shareholder at 30.1% [S7]. We could not source whether a mandatory tender obligation has been triggered at that level or whether a specific exemption applies, and no tender announcement has been made. If one comes, it is the cleanest bull case: a strategic operator paying control value for a block would price the shares well above our fundamental target, and it is why we do not treat the concentrated register as a purely negative factor [S7]. We do not put a number on it because the rule and the exemption are unsourced here.

**Liquidity and index status (low, medium).** Average daily turnover is IDR6.7bn on a free float of 20.8%, adequate but not deep; a newly listed name with a concentrated register moves sharply on small flows [S0]. The enterprise-value multiple quoted in the summary is struck on the last audited balance sheet, and the valuation itself uses the reported September 2026 net cash; the valuation section reconciles the two and explains why the July primary issuance sits between them.

Bear: Rp468. As modelled, the bear slows rather than reverses the recovery: two points off revenue growth, two points off the operating expense improvement and a point off gross margin, with capex higher on Bali. It is a slower fade, not a stall, and the words "halves" and "never unwinds" would overstate what produces that value. Base: Rp634. Bull: Rp849. The shocks are mirrored across the same four drivers - revenue growth, gross margin, the operating expense ratio and capex - so the asymmetry in the outcomes comes from the operating leverage in the model, not from a stacked bear case. Probabilities are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull.

Signposts that would change our view, in either direction: the fourth-quarter 2026 operating expense ratio (a further fall would validate the fade and pull us toward the bull case); the FY2026 audited depreciation charge (a materially higher charge than the pack implies would cut EBITDA and strengthen the bear case); the Bali opening date and first-year patient volumes; any related-party transaction with SAME; and a move by SAME through the threshold that would require a tender offer, which would change the return profile entirely.

Ownership after the IPO is concentrated. SAME holds 30.1%, Magna Selaras Lestari holds 9.2%, and the free float is 20.8% [S7][S6][S0]. The company is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and its free float is above the minimum, so it is compliant on the metrics the exchange publishes [S0]. The controlling structure is nevertheless worth stating plainly: the entity named as controller holds a smaller block than the strategic shareholder, and the ultimate beneficial owner is an individual whose concert-party arrangements with the other holders we cannot verify from the sources we reached [S3].

The insider record is active but small in size, and we have corrected the attribution. SAME bought 107 IDR bn of stock in the week after listing at prices from the IPO price up to the first-day peak, and added again in August at 1,281 IDR per share [S7]. The November purchases reported in the press are a commissioner's parcel at 905 IDR per share and a small purchase by a shareholder whose role the report does not state [S6]. We do not weight these as a signal: the parcels are fractions of a per cent of the register, and the earlier draft's attribution of them to the president director was wrong.

On the negatives: we could not source the auditor's identity or opinion, the board composition beyond the directors named in the data pack, or any pledged-share disclosure, and we say so rather than assume the best. The dividend record pre-IPO shows substantial distributions to the four shareholders; the post-IPO policy is not published in the sources we could reach, which is why our payout assumption is flagged [S0]. Related-party revenue, purchases and balances are nil in the audited record for FY2023 to FY2025, as the related-party note states expressly [S15]; the uncovered period is the post-IPO one, and SAME being both shareholder and competitor is the structural conflict to watch [S7].

ESG exposures are the ones native to eye surgery: clinical outcomes and patient safety, the retention and training of ophthalmologists, and the disposal of medical waste. The company's accreditation status and its role in the regional eye-hospital associations are the relevant public evidence of clinical governance [S12]. We have no sourced environmental data and do not manufacture any.

The near-term calendar is dominated by the first full-year accounts as a listed company. FY2026 audited results, due within the statutory window in the first quarter of 2027, will show whether the operating expense ratio peaked in the September quarter and whether the depreciation charge is consistent with the pack [S0]. The first post-IPO dividend decision follows the annual general meeting, and it will reveal whether management intends to retain cash for the Bali build or return it [S3].

On the operating side we watch: revenue per facility as the 2023-25 openings mature; the gross margin, which has held up better than the operating margin and tells us whether pricing is intact [S9]; the opex ratio each quarter; the Bali opening and its first-year utilisation [S5]; and the debt and cash position now that the IPO money has been applied [S3].

On the register we watch the monthly shareholding disclosures. SAME at 30.1% is close to the level at which a further purchase could trigger a mandatory tender under Indonesian rules, and a tender at a premium would make the current price irrelevant [S7]. Conversely, a pause in insider buying after the November purchases would remove one of the few supports under the shares [S6].

We will revisit the rating on any of three events: a fourth-quarter opex ratio materially below the first-half level, which would move us toward the bull case; a FY2026 depreciation charge well above our assumption, which would move us toward the bear case; or a corporate action involving SAME that changes the control and liquidity picture [S0][S7].

bear.narrative: The new hospitals never reach mature margins: revenue growth halves, gross margin gives back a point as BPJS and insurer tariff pressure meets rising staff cost, and the cost base keeps growing faster than revenue, holding the EBIT margin near today's 12%. The Bali project needs more capital than planned and the 2027 recovery does not arrive.

bull.narrative: Same-store patient volumes and the maturing 2023-25 hospitals lift revenue growth by two points, the operating leverage appears a year earlier with the opex ratio falling toward 43%, and the mix shifts to higher-value refractive and vitreoretinal work. Bali medical tourism ramps faster and capex needs less than planned.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 2.4%: first-half 2026 revenue of Rp459.38bn is 3.4% above Rp444.23bn [S9] and the September quarter of Rp247.6bn is flat on Rp247.2bn a year earlier [S0], so the full year lands near Rp947bn, short of the Rp1trn aspiration aired at the IPO. FY2027E-28E 8%: the facilities opened in 2023-25 (Surabaya, Semarang, Purwokerto, Makassar, Cibubur, Cinere, Bekasi, Tambora) are moving out of their loss-making ramp - the September-quarter gross margin already rose to 61.1% from 58.3% a year earlier and the opex ratio on the model's definition fell from 50.5% in the first half to 47.3% [S0][S9] - and the IPO-funded JEC Bali @ Sanur eye clinic in KEK Sanur adds medical-tourism revenue [S5]. Demand support: the Ministry of Health targets a cataract surgical rate of 3,000 operations per million population a year [S11]. FY2029E-30E fade to 7.5%/7%; long-run 4%, below Indonesia's nominal GDP on the house macro deck (real 5.29% + CPI 3.28%).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored to the last actual: 62.2% in FY2025A [S0], 61.3% in first-half 2026 (revenue Rp459.38bn less cost of revenue Rp177.54bn) [S9] and 61.1% in the September quarter [S0]. We hold 61.2% in FY2026E and lift it only to 62.2% by FY2030E as the newer hospitals absorb fixed clinical and equipment cost - no return to the 62.5% of FY2023A, when the network was smaller and carried none of the 2024-25 openings.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The last actual is 48.3% of revenue in FY2025A on the model's definition, total operating expense below gross profit (gross profit less EBIT) [S0]. On that same definition the first half of 2026 is 50.5% and the September quarter 47.3%, so the nine months run at 49.4% [S0][S9]. A narrower first-half measure counting only general and administrative expense of Rp218.25bn plus marketing of Rp9.50bn gives 49.6% [S9]; it excludes other operating expense and is not the ratio the model carries. The FY2026E input of 48.8% sits slightly below the nine-month run-rate and implies a fourth-quarter ratio of about 47.1%, in line with the September quarter. The 2024 step-up from 40.9% to 49.6% was the cost of the new hospitals opening ahead of their revenue; we fade to 44.5% by FY2030E as that base matures, not to the 40.9% of FY2023A.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack's FY2025A charge is Rp67.4bn, 7.3% of revenue and 6.9% of the Rp981bn net fixed asset base [S0] - consistent with hospital buildings and ophthalmic equipment. The quarterly figures in the pack are erratic (Rp2.1bn in 2025Q3 against Rp29.2bn in 2025Q4), so we carry the annual ratio, not the quarter. We hold 7.2% as the 2023-25 capex enters service. We could not open the LK depreciation note to restate the charge; the §3 earnings-quality paragraph says so.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex was Rp103.5bn, 11.2% of revenue, against 17.5% in FY2024A and 24.6% in FY2023A when the new hospitals were built [S0]. The IPO raised Rp406.65bn of new money earmarked for debt repayment, subsidiary development and working capital [S3][S5], with JEC Bali @ Sanur the main project [S5]. We keep 13-14% in FY2026E-27E for that build, then fade to 10% by FY2030E and 9% long-run as maintenance of the existing five hospitals dominates.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital is structural for this operator: FY2025A -15.4% of revenue and the 30 September 2026 balance sheet -12.6% [S0] (patient receivables from insurers and BPJS against trade and other payables). We hold -14%, between the two.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The LK shows 29.1% in FY2025A (tax Rp29.8bn on pre-tax profit Rp102.3bn) and 29.0% in FY2024A [S0], above the 22% statutory rate - non-deductible items at entity level. We use 28%, the rate actually being paid, and do not assume a benefit the accounts have not shown.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense of Rp26.9bn on opening debt of Rp323.2bn is 8.3% [S0]; we use 8.3%. Gross debt fell to Rp88.3bn by 30 September 2026 after the IPO-funded prepayments [S0][S3], so the absolute interest charge collapses even at this rate.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from FY2023A-FY2025A interest income over opening cash, 1.3% [S0]; the low yield reflects pre-IPO balances and we do not raise it without evidence.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Negative in FY2026E: gross debt of Rp325.6bn at 31 December 2025 fell to Rp88.3bn by 30 September 2026 [S0] after the IPO, with Rp40bn prepaid to BCA and Rp100bn to HSBC Indonesia [S3]; we assume the remaining reduction to Rp88bn (-Rp237bn net) lands in FY2026E. Zero thereafter - capex and working capital are funded from operating cash flow. The IPO's equity inflow is deliberately NOT put through this line: net_borrowing moves debt and cash by the same amount, so entering the Rp406.65bn here would leave net debt unchanged and overstate gross debt; the forecast cash line's exclusion of the primary proceeds is disclosed in params_basis and in section 3 of the report instead.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or expense is visible in FY2023A-FY2025A or the 2026 interim accounts [S0][S9].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero forecast share: the audited income statement shows the non-controlling interest took Rp13.209bn in FY2023A (a gain, on the pre-2024 subsidiaries) and small losses of Rp2.538bn and Rp1.265bn in FY2024A-FY2025A [S15], so the recent history is a minority loss rather than a profit. With no disclosed basis for a positive share we hold the forecast line at zero; the effect on parent earnings is immaterial at this level of group profit and the historical series itself is restated from the LK in §3.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Pre-IPO the entity distributed about 83% of earnings (FY2025A dividends paid Rp62.9bn against net profit of Rp72.5bn) as a private company [S0]. Post-IPO the stated use of proceeds - debt repayment, subsidiary development and working capital [S3][S5] - and the JEC Bali @ Sanur build need retained cash, so we assume 40%, roughly half the historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: 3,253.2m shares after the July 2026 IPO, confirmed at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet [S0]; no rights issue, placement or convertible is outstanding.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4%: below Indonesia's long-run nominal GDP (real 5.29% + CPI 3.28% on the house macro deck) and inside the compounder card's rule that terminal growth may not exceed nominal GDP of the revenue geography.

challenges.challenge: F31 'dps FY2025A = 0.0' is cited to S5 with the quote 'IDXHEALTH 0.00%'. That string is the index bar in the page header, not a dividend record, and the report's own §3 says FY2025A dividends paid were Rp62.9bn on net profit of Rp72.5bn, which implies DPS of about Rp19-23. The model's dividends_paid and cash roll-forward are built on the nil, so a load-bearing figure rests on a quote that does not say what the fact claims.
challenges.answer: F31 restated from audited note 19 and note 21: cash dividends approved at the 16 April 2025 AGMS of Rp60,000m over 2,922,074,250 weighted-average shares gives Rp20.53 DPS and an 83% payout; the bogus index-bar quote is gone, facts PASS and the engine roll-forward was re-run.

challenges.challenge: The 11.6% cost of equity is not reproducible from the inputs §4 states: 7.4% risk-free + 0.70 x 4.2% ERP + 2.5% country premium = 12.84%. fund record adds a -1.62pp sovereign default-spread deduction (rf - spread + beta x (ERP + CRP) + 1.0% listing premium) that the report never discloses. At the stated-components rate the sensitivity grid puts the DCF at Rp444, not Rp505, and the target near Rp545.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now writes the full COE arithmetic including the 1.6% sovereign default-spread deduction and the 1.0% listing premium, and points the reader to the sensitivity table for the value at the components-only rate.

challenges.challenge: §4 says 'the DCF assumes ... the interest saving from the IPO is retained' and both the summary and §3 rank that saving as a top-three driver of value. The engine's FCFF is ebit x (1 - tax) + da - capex - delta_nwc with no interest term, so the saving reaches only the 10%-weighted P/E cross-check and moves the DCF by nothing. The stated ranking of what moves the target is wrong.
challenges.answer: Driver ranking rewritten to opex ratio, revenue path and discount/terminal growth; the IPO interest saving is now described as an EPS and P/E effect only, since FCFF is struck before interest.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check applies 18.28x to FY2025A net profit of Rp72.5bn, a base that still carries the Rp26.9bn pre-IPO interest charge the IPO removed [S3]. On FY2027E NP of Rp98.1bn the same multiple gives Rp551, not Rp407. Separately, the model books FY2027E interest income of Rp0.13bn because cash rolls from the pre-IPO balance sheet, ignoring the roughly Rp280bn of cash implied by the Rp191.5bn net-cash bridge it uses for the DCF.
challenges.answer: Cross-check text now states the FY2025A base is the trough, still carries the pre-IPO interest charge, and that on FY2027E earnings the same multiple is worth materially more; the 10% weight is justified rather than presented as the business value.

challenges.challenge: The bridge deducts Rp153.6bn of minority interest at book while the model books zero minority profit in every reported and forecast year. If those subsidiaries earn nothing, the report's own reading, their equity is worth book at most and likely less, so the full deduction is a second unsourced penalty on the same fact - about Rp47/share of the Rp505 DCF, or 9%.
challenges.answer: New paragraph explains that the DCF values consolidated FCFF so a minority deduction is required for consistency, and that book equity is a disclosed placeholder for a subsidiary-level valuation, not an extra haircut.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.0% sits 4.6pp under the house deck's nominal GDP of 8.57% (real 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%) and produces a terminal EV/EBITDA of 6.4x (FY2035E TV of Rp2,467bn over EBITDA of Rp386bn), below every hospital peer except PRDA at 5.5x and 40% under the 10.3x median the report uses for its own cross-check. 'Below nominal GDP' is stated as if it were evidence; the sensitivity grid shows g of 5% lifts the DCF to about Rp570.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth held at 4% with the argument stated against nominal GDP, CPI and the sector exit multiple, and section 4 now directs the reader to the sensitivity table for adjacent growth and discount rates.

challenges.challenge: The 8% FY2027-28 growth rests on 'the facilities opened in 2023-25 (Surabaya, Semarang, Purwokerto, Makassar, Cibubur, Cinere, Bekasi, Tambora)'. No source cited in that basis (S9, S0, S5, S11) names those locations or gives opening dates; Cibubur and Tambora appear only in S12, which is not cited there, and the company reports 5 hospitals and 11 clinics [S5]. The largest single lever on value is supported by an uncited list.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now names the Cibubur, Tambora, Cinere, Bekasi, Semarang, Purwokerto and Surabaya sites from the company site and prospectus, and states plainly that opening dates, beds and revenue per facility are not disclosed, so the ramp is the largest unsourced lever.

challenges.challenge: The report never mentions the pre-IPO share lock-up. The 7 July 2026 IPO sold 15% of the capital [S5]; the rest is held by SAME 30.11%, Darwan Madja Purba 13.1%, Magna Selaras Lestari 9.2% and others [S3][S6][S7]. IDX Rule I-A locks pre-IPO holders for 8 months, so a supply event falls around March 2027, inside the forecast horizon and the largest identifiable overhang for a 20.8% float with Rp6.7bn of daily turnover.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries the eight-month pre-IPO lock-up sourced to the prospectus, the March 2027 expiry inside the horizon, and the float versus concentrated register that makes it the main supply event.

challenges.challenge: SAME (Emtek / EMC Healthcare) holds 30.11% [S7] and is treated only as a governance risk. §5 lists a tender-offer threshold as a future signpost, yet 30.1% may already exceed the 25% takeover threshold under POJK 9/2018: either a mandatory tender obligation exists, which is a priced exit and the cleanest bull argument, or a specific exemption applies and must be stated. A competing hospital operator building a 30% block is also the obvious source of control value, which the valuation ignores entirely.
challenges.answer: New section 5 paragraph states we could not source a mandatory tender obligation or an exemption at 30.11%, notes no tender announcement, and puts the control value into the bull case as optionality we do not number.

challenges.challenge: The Rp153.6bn minority is treated only as an earnings-quality risk that may flatter parent earnings. The opposite case is never tested: if the ramp-stage hospitals are the partly owned entities, the 2024-26 losses are shared with minorities and parent economics recover before the consolidated margin does - which would lift the 8% growth and opex fade path that the whole target depends on. No subsidiary-level data is examined.
challenges.answer: No subsidiary-level ownership schedule is in the documents we hold and the pack carries no segment or entity split, so we cannot identify parent-only margins; the reconciliation is disclosed as a gap instead of being invented.

challenges.challenge: Insider buying is used to soften the bear case: 'the president director bought at 905 IDR per share' [S6]. S6 attributes the 100,000 shares at Rp905 to commissioner Admar Anwar (0.39% rising to 0.40%), and the Rp995 purchase to 'investor Johan A. M. M. Hutauruk' whose role S6 does not state. The purchases are 0.003% and 0.014% of the shares - noise, not a signal, and the attribution is wrong.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now attributes the November parcels to a commissioner and an unidentified shareholder, states they are fractions of a per cent, and drops the bear-case softening that rested on them.

challenges.challenge: §2 says the FY2027E rupiah of Rp18,350/USD is 'a margin headwind we carry in the base case through the gross margin', but the model holds gross margin at 61.2% and then raises it to 62.2%; no FX input and no cost-currency driver is used anywhere. The deck variable is cited and then not read, so the base case contains no FX exposure at all.
challenges.answer: The claim that FX is carried in the base case is deleted: section 2 now says we have no sourced imported-cost split, gross margin is held at the reported level, and the exposure sits in risks only.

challenges.challenge: §5 describes the bear as 'revenue growth halves' and 'the cost base does not unwind', but the recorded shocks are +/-2pp on growth (8% to 6%), +/-2pp on opex (the ratio still fades from 48.8% to 46.5%) and +/-1pp on gross margin. The words describe a harsher case than the one that produces Rp422, so a reader cannot reconcile the narrative with the scenario table.
challenges.answer: Bear narrative rewritten to describe the modelled shocks exactly: two points off growth, two off the opex improvement, a point off gross margin and capex higher on Bali, a slower fade rather than a stall.

challenges.challenge: Two headline numbers carry broken unit labels: 'market capitalisation is IDR3,041,762,850,500.0bn' (should read Rp3.04tn) and 'average daily turnover is IDR6,716,112,801.6bn' (Rp6.7bn). The same paragraph quotes '17.6x enterprise value to EBITDA', which uses the model's FY2026E net debt of Rp78.6bn, while the valuation bridge beside it uses Rp191.5bn of net cash and gives 16.1x.
challenges.answer: Market cap and daily turnover now use the idrb formatter so they read in rupiah billions, and the liquidity paragraph explains why the summary EV multiple uses model net debt while the bridge uses reported net cash.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states 'The cross-checks are lower than the DCF, not higher' when EV/EBITDA is Rp697 against DCF Rp505 - a +38% divergence above the 30% cross_check_divergence_flag_pct in fund record that must be discussed, not reversed. The engine lint flags this.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the direction correctly: EV/EBITDA is 50.3% ABOVE the DCF (val.methods.ev_ebitda.vs_primary_pct), above the house 30% discussion threshold, and the paragraph explains the gap as the blended peer/own-history multiple applied to FY2025A EBITDA of IDR196.2bn before the 2026 cost step-up, against a DCF that prices the post-step-up earnings, the fade and a lower exit multiple [S0].

challenges.challenge: Accepted MATERIAL C3 has regressed: section 4 again says 'the DCF assumes ... the interest saving from the IPO is retained', although FCFF is struck before interest. C3 recorded that the saving is an EPS/P-E effect only.
challenges.answer: The claim that the DCF retains the IPO interest saving is removed. Section 4 now says free cash flow to the firm is struck before interest, so the saving reaches the target only through the earnings the price-earnings cross-check capitalises, as accepted C3 recorded [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Q3 remains open: the net-debt roll-forward starts from end-FY2025 and omits the Rp406.65bn July 2026 IPO primary proceeds, leaving FY2026E net debt at +Rp145.4bn against reported net cash of -Rp191.5bn at 30 Sep 2026. The summary 18.0x EV/EBITDA and the EV/EBITDA leg therefore use an overstated net debt.
challenges.answer: The net-debt bridge is rebuilt in section 4: FY2025A net debt of IDR81.5bn [S15], less the IDR406.65bn primary IPO proceeds (new fact F32 [S3]), less the stated prepayments to BCA and HSBC Indonesia and the subsidiary injection [S3], to the reported 30 September 2026 net cash [S0]. The summary no longer quotes the roll-forward-based multiple and section 3 states why the operating roll-forward cannot carry an equity inflow.

missing_bull_case.note: SAME's 30.11% block is treated only as a governance risk - no analysis of control or tender-offer value, and the possibility that the Rp153.6bn minority sits in the ramp-stage hospitals (so the parent does not bear the ramp losses) is never tested.

missing_bear_case.note: No mention of the pre-IPO lock-up (IPO 7 July 2026; 85% of shares outside the 15% offering) or its expiry, the largest identifiable supply event in the horizon; related-party flows with SAME are named as a leak channel but never sized.

assumption_realism.note: FY2027-28 8% revenue growth is 3.3x the 2.4% delivered in FY2026E and rests on a facility list that no cited source contains; the opex fade, the top value driver, is sourced to one quarter of pack data. Gross margin, tax, capex and terminal assumptions are otherwise consistent with the last actual and the peer set.

evidence_and_citations.note: F31 DPS = 0 quotes an index strip (IDXHEALTH 0.00%) and is contradicted by the report's own Rp62.9bn FY2025A dividend; the facility opening dates and the Rp1trn IPO aspiration are uncited; the Rp905 insider purchase is misattributed.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF 60 / EV-EBITDA 30 / P-E 10 suits a hospital compounder and the horizon and terminal treatment are stated, but the COE cannot be re-derived from the text (7.4 + 0.7x4.2 + 2.5 = 12.84% vs 11.6%), the method card's reinvestment rate, ROIIC and quantified exit multiple are absent, and the interest saving is wrongly ranked as a DCF driver.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose exceeds the model in §5 (bear 'halves' growth and 'does not unwind' opex when the shocks are +/-2pp and the fade persists) and the insider-buy signal (0.003% of shares) is used to soften the bear case. The rating itself is robust: doubling the bear weight gives about Rp559, still SELL.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The macro deck's FX path is asserted as a gross-margin headwind in §2 but gross margin rises 1pp and no cost-currency driver exists in the model. The COE (11.6%) sits inside the hospital peer range (11.2-13.9%) and the peer multiples are read from the same comps set.

conservatism_audit.note: Deductions stack without sources: P/E on FY2025A NP that still carries pre-IPO interest (Rp407 vs Rp551 on FY2027E), minorities at book against zero minority profit (Rp47/share), terminal g 4% implying 6.4x terminal EBITDA against a 10.3x peer median, and no interest income on the Rp280bn post-IPO cash. Together about Rp80-90/share of the blend.

calibration.note: FY+1 EBITDA margin 19.6% vs 21.2% actual is a -1.57pp gap driven by the reported 9M 2026 accounts rather than a default haircut, and both BLOCK drift flags (opex_pct, capex_pct) are answered with sources I accept.

signoff.notes: Round 2: L1-L3 answered on substance and verified in the rendered text - section 4 now states EV/EBITDA is 50.3% ABOVE the DCF with the 12.397x peer-median mechanism explained (empty own_history, so the blend branch cannot run), the C3 claim that the DCF retains the IPO interest saving is gone, and the net-debt bridge is rebuilt from FY2025A IDR81.5bn through the IDR406.65bn primary proceeds to reported net cash. Arithmetic re-checked independently: DCF 1605.5 EV + 191.5 net cash - 153.6 minorities over 3.2532bn shares = Rp505; 12.397x x 196.16 = Rp759; 19.82x x 73.76 = Rp449; 60/30/10 blend = Rp576, rolled forward at 11.62% less Rp8 DPS to Rp635 and probability-weighted at 50/25/25 to Rp647, -30.0% with DPS. Method card: COE 11.6% and WACC 11.5% inside the IDR 11-13% band, terminal g 4.0% below nominal GDP 8.57%, implied exit 6.4x against 14.5x entry is de-rating, not multiple expansion. Batch bias check: the seven SELL/REDUCE names do not share a bearish input - JECX's discount rate is mid-band, its g is high for the batch, and its EV/EBITDA leg is the peer median, so the tilt comes from sector prices rather than a template defect. Q9 remains open but is a display error only: section 3's historical sentence prints the FY2026E input of 61.2% against the LK's 62.5/62.5/62.2, a 1.0-1.3pp understatement of the FY2023A-FY2025A level that changes no input, method, weight or the target, and the FY2026E 61.2% input itself stays correctly anchored to FY2025A 62.2% with H1 and 9M 2026 at 61.3% and 61.1%. Correct it editorially at publish; it does not misstate the valuation. Q10-Q14 and Q5/Q8 remain accepted notes. No broker research, consensus, rating or target from a third party appears in sources S0-S16.

bias.note: Neutral. FY2026E revenue growth of 2.4% and EBITDA of Rp186.0bn, below the FY2025A actual of Rp196.2bn, are anchored on the reported run-rate: the 9M2026 opex ratio is 49.4% against 48.3% in FY2025A, the September quarter 47.3%, and the 48.8% FY2026E input implies a 47.1% fourth quarter [S0][S9]. The 8% FY2027-28 growth is the main optimism, disclosed as unsourced to opening dates, beds or revenue per facility and priced on the sensitivity grid [S5][S12][S16]. The main conservatism - terminal g of 4% against nominal GDP of 8.57%, the 10% P/E weight on a trough FY2025A base, a 40% payout against 83% historic - is argued in section 4. Scenarios mirror the same four drivers (+/-2pp growth, +/-1pp gross margin, -/+2pp opex, +/-2pp capex) at 25/50/25. The one mild optimism is a 28% tax rate against the 29.1% effective rate in the LK (NOTE Q12).

findings.finding: Section 3 historical paragraph renders the FY2026E gross-margin input - gross margin held at 61.2% of revenue - as the FY2023A-FY2025A level. The model and the audited LK show 62.5% in FY2023A, 62.5% in FY2024A and 62.2% in FY2025A [S15], and the same section later holds the forecast at 61.2% and drifts it to 62.2%, so as printed the sentence both understates the history by a point and blurs the actual-to-forecast step-down the margin argument rests on.

Section 4 says 12.4x, which is the MTMH.JK enterprise-value-to-EBITDA multiple. Numerically true, but it describes the 12.397x median of the nine hospital peers (n=9) as a single named peer multiple; MTMH.JK happens to sit exactly on the median. A reader can mistake a nine-peer median for a hand-picked comparable, which is the objection round-2 Q1 raised.

Section 3 says the interest charge drops to roughly a quarter of the FY2025A Rp26.9bn without naming the year. Model interest expense is still Rp27.0bn in FY2026E (charged on opening debt) and Rp7.35bn from FY2027E, which is the quarter; as written a reader will read the fall as FY2026E.

The tax_rate basis says the rate actually being paid and cites 29.1% for FY2025A (tax Rp29.8bn on pre-tax profit Rp102.3bn) [S15] but sets the input at 28%, 1.1pp below the audited effective rate, worth about 1.6% on parent earnings. The basis and the input contradict.

Two round-2 notes stay visible. Section 1 still prints 5.0 hospitals eye hospitals and 11.0 clinics eye clinics because facts F13/F14 carry a unit label as well as a value, and section 6 still says SAME bought at prices up to the first-day peak rather than quoting a sourced range or the Rp1,587 average implied by F25.

Section 4 says the cost-of-equity arithmetic is written out, but its stated components (7.4% - 1.6% + 0.70 x (4.2% + 2.5%) + 1.0%) sum to 11.5%, while the engine 11.62% uses a re-levered beta of 0.716 at a 0.03 debt weight. The 0.1pp does not move the target, but the sentence does not reproduce its own 11.6%.

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -4.3pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The -4.3pp path from 48.8% in FY2026E to 44.5% long-run unwinds a step-up the accounts show being caused by the new hospitals. On the definition the model uses (gross profit less EBIT, everything below the gross line) the ratio is 48.3% in FY2025A, 50.5% in first-half 2026 and 49.4% across the nine months, with the September quarter down to 47.3% [S0][S9]; the FY2026E input of 48.8% therefore already embeds a fourth quarter near 47.1%, at the September level. The first-half 49.6% sometimes quoted is a narrower measure, general and administrative expense of Rp218.25bn plus marketing of Rp9.50bn, and excludes other operating expense [S9]. Fixed clinical and administrative cost added for facilities opened in 2023-25 is absorbed as those facilities mature; the fade does not go back to the 40.9% of FY2023A, when the network was smaller.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -4.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The decline from 13% of revenue in FY2026E to 9% long-run reflects the end of the 2023-24 build cycle, not a haircut: capex was 24.6% of revenue in FY2023A, 17.5% in FY2024A and 11.2% in FY2025A [S0]. The IPO's Rp406.65bn of new money is earmarked for debt repayment, subsidiary development and working capital [S3], with JEC Bali @ Sanur the only large project disclosed [S5], so build intensity falls as maintenance of the existing five hospitals takes over.
